threads.body: This test’s assertions are conditional on an external system property, so running it from an IDE (or under a different Gradle task) may only exercise one branch and not clearly communicate which behavior is being verified. Consider splitting into two tests (default-off vs explicit opt-in) and using JUnit conditions/annotations (e.g., enabled/disabled-if-system-property) or separate test classes so each test has a single, unconditional expectation.

This test’s assertions are conditional on an external system property, so running it from an IDE (or under a different Gradle task) may only exercise one branch and not clearly communicate which behavior is being verified. Consider splitting into two tests (default-off vs explicit opt-in) and using JUnit conditions/annotations (e.g., enabled/disabled-if-system-property) or separate test classes so each test has a single, unconditional expectation.

The test enablement relies on a hard-coded task name check (`name != "testDisabled"`), which is brittle (renames/new tasks can change behavior silently). Prefer configuring enablement explicitly for the specific tasks that need it (e.g., `named<Test>("test")`, `named<Test>("testExperimental")`, etc.) or matching a small allow-list of task names, so new Test tasks don’t accidentally inherit “enabled=true”.

Using `jvmArgs("-D...")` works, but Gradle’s `systemProperty("otel.instrumentation.hystrix.enabled", "true")` is the more direct API for setting `-D` properties, and tends to be clearer/less error-prone when multiple `jvmArgs` are composed. Consider switching to `systemProperty(...)` for consistency with other test configuration (you already use `systemProperty("collectMetadata", ...)`).
